summary:
Bolu is a province of Türkiye and sits entirely under the national framework that governs LGBT rights across the country. The pattern is one of documented, institutionalised state hostility rather than informal prejudice. Kaos GL's 2025 human-rights monitoring recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions of which 256 were recorded through formal channels and 43 were taken off the record.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported in October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', with penalties of up to three years in prison, and would criminalise participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years. Human Rights Watch described the draft as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but enforcement of prohibitions that exist only on paper is already documented in practice.

The draft also reaches transition-related care. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, and make permanent infertility a condition of eligibility. Health professionals who perform such care would face penalties including fines and prison terms of up to seven years, and patients would face terms of up to three years.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, found that hostility became explicit state policy during the year: senior officials issued hate speech, instructions were issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The report documented six right-to-life violations, three of which rights organisations classified as hate-motivated killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. It also recorded 89 cases of torture or ill-treatment, up from 51 the previous year.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the practical effect of that policy. In one large city in 2025, police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the streets, in shops and in cafés and held them at a police station for 'General Information Gathering' background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that police took no fines but documented her anyway, and noted that the new law had not been passed even as its prohibitions were being applied to her.

Foreign visitors carry a specific exposure at every checkpoint. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any interaction with police in Bolu province is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk for a trans visitor whose passport gender marker does not match how they appear.

Violence in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in the Bakırköy district of Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Prison conditions remain among the most severe points of risk for any trans person detained in Türkiye. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in six cities demanded an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison.

The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening at ministry level. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
Turbulence is concentrated at the level of pending legislation rather than enacted change. The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft when reported, and its status after October 2025 is unresolved in the sources available here. Its provisions have nonetheless shaped enforcement already in operation, a pattern in which authorities act on prohibitions that are not yet law.

The political frame is explicitly family-centred. Human Rights Watch identifies the government's language of protecting 'the family' and 'public morals' as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people, and the 'Year of the Family' banner is the mechanism through which that framing reached public institutions.

Ten years of Pride-week violations provide the comparative baseline. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The depth of the regime is historical as well as current. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Contest exists but is largely formal. Opposition members of parliament have raised trans prison conditions directly, and a cross-city coordination of Human Rights Association branches has demanded independent investigation, while the Human Rights Association, the Turkish Medical Association and fifteen LGBT organisations have lodged objections to the draft package.
localsOnly:
Turkish residents face the same legal instruments described above, and the resident-facing exposure is wider than the visitor-facing one because residents are subject to long-term record-keeping. The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation removes the 'other' option from hospital records and requires medical-board e-reports to cite 'gender reassignment' explicitly, which places transition care in identifiable official files.

Trans residents detained are placed in facilities by registered sex rather than gender identity. The parliament case raised on 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Detention leaves a documented trace even where no penalty follows. In the 2025 urban stop-and-search operations, trans women were documented at police stations under background-check procedures without being fined, which means the encounter enters police records regardless of outcome.

Complaint mechanisms against prison conditions are ineffective according to the Prison Insider profile, can attract further violence, and are weakened by transfers that sever visits and solidarity networks. There is no staff training on LGBT needs and administration operates on a binary basis.

Kaos GL's 2025 counts are monitoring-based and rely on formal reporting channels, with an acknowledged off-record component of detentions. Residents who are never reported generate no count.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no documentation specific to Bolu. No province-level police practice, incident, facility, clinic, hate-crime outcome, complaint procedure or municipal policy is recorded for Bolu, and none is asserted here.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package after its October 2025 reporting is unresolved. The sources available describe a leaked draft that had not been passed; whether it has since been tabled, amended or enacted is not sourced.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation remains in force, and whether hospitals in Bolu province apply its reporting requirements, is not sourced.

Penalty figures cited for the draft package vary across reporting levels, with ceremony offences at up to four years and general conduct offences at up to three years. These are proposed provisions, not current law, and should not be read as enacted sentences.

Kaos GL's figures depend on reporting channels that undercount off-record enforcement by design, and the 2025 total may therefore be a floor rather than a ceiling.

Local access to transition-related care in Bolu, the identity documents accepted at Bolu checkpoints, and the operation of any provincial health directorate circular are not sourced. A trans visitor should treat the national framework described here as fully applicable in Bolu in the absence of evidence to the contrary.
